blocks.text: A cable winch on a crane lowers a 50 kg load, and the cable tension is not simply the load's weight: the drum has inertia, the load is accelerating and the tension falls below $mg$. A drive wheel has the same trap: the friction force at the ground both pushes the vehicle and spins the wheel. Constraints link these motions, and kinetics must use them.

blocks.markdown: Planar kinetics gives three equations per body: $\sum F_x=ma_{Gx}$, $\sum F_y=ma_{Gy}$ and $\sum M_G=I_G\alpha$. When bodies are linked by a rope or by rolling contact, the unknowns outnumber the equations until the **kinematic constraint** is added. Take $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ and use SI throughout (forces in N, masses in kg, $I$ in kg m$^2$).

blocks.title: Rolling without slip
blocks.text: The contact point of a wheel of radius $R$ has zero velocity relative to the ground, so the centre acceleration and angular acceleration are linked by $a_G=R\alpha$. The friction force there is static, not kinetic, and satisfies $F\le\mu_sN$. It does no work on a body that really does not slip.

blocks.caption: Rolling constraint and the no-slip friction limit.

blocks.title: Cylinder pulled at its axle
blocks.prompt: A solid cylinder (mass 20 kg, radius 0.25 m, $I_G=\tfrac12mR^2$) rolls without slip on a horizontal floor under a horizontal force $P=60$ N applied at its centre. Find $a_G$, the friction force and the minimum $\mu_s$.

steps.text: Translation (friction $F$ acts backward at the contact point).
Rotation about $G$: only $F$ has a moment, $FR=I_G\alpha=\tfrac12mR^2(a_G/R)$, so $F=\tfrac12ma_G$.

blocks.markdown: **Winch drum.** A load of mass $m$ hangs on a cable wound on a drum of radius $r$ and inertia $I$ about its axle. The cable does not slip or stretch, so the load acceleration equals the drum rim acceleration, $a=r\alpha$. For the load (down positive) $mg-T=ma$. For the drum $Tr=I\alpha=Ia/r$.

blocks.caption: Eliminate $T$ to get $a$; the term $I/r^2$ is the drum's equivalent mass.

blocks.title: Lowering a load
blocks.prompt: A 50 kg load is lowered by a cable on a drum of radius 0.25 m with $I=2.0$ kg m$^2$ (no brake, no bearing friction). Find the acceleration and cable tension.

steps.text: Tension from the drum equation, checked with the load equation.

blocks.answer: $a=5.98$ m/s$^2$ downward and $T=191$ N, far less than the 490.5 N weight.

rows: $T=$ same on both sides of a light cable
blocks.caption: Constraints that close the equation set.

blocks.markdown: **Off-centre mass on a pin.** A member pinned at O whose centre of mass G is a distance $e$ from O moves in a circle of radius $e$. Its centre-of-mass acceleration has a normal part $e\omega^2$ (toward O) and a tangential part $e\alpha$. The pin reactions must supply the net force $ma_G$, and the driving moment about O is $I_O\alpha$ with $I_O=I_G+me^2$.

blocks.caption: Components of the pin force in the normal and tangential directions (gravity is excluded when the axis is vertical).

blocks.title: Unbalanced rotor
blocks.prompt: A rotor on a vertical shaft has $m=6$ kg, $e=0.04$ m and $I_G=0.03$ kg m$^2$. At the instant considered $\omega=50$ rad/s and $\alpha=400$ rad/s$^2$. Find the pin reaction and the driving moment about the shaft.

steps.text: Moment about O with $I_O=0.03+6(0.04)^2=0.0396$ kg m$^2$.

blocks.answer: Pin force about 608 N and driving moment about 15.8 N m. The normal part dominates because it grows with $\omega^2$.

blocks.title: Order of attack
blocks.text: Draw the free-body diagram, write the three equations, add the constraint ($a=R\alpha$ or $a=r\alpha$ or $a_G=e\alpha$), then solve. Check afterwards that friction does not exceed $\mu_sN$ if no slip is claimed.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Assuming the cable tension equals $mg$ while the load accelerates, using $F=\mu N$ when the wheel rolls without slip (it is only $F\le\mu_sN$), and taking moments about O but using $I_G$ instead of $I_O$.

points: Rolling without slip adds the constraint $a_G=R\alpha$; the static friction force is whatever the equations demand and must stay within $\mu_sN$.
For a winch, $a=mg/(m+I/r^2)$ and the tension is less than $mg$ whenever the load accelerates downward.
An off-centre centre of mass at distance $e$ gives pin force components $me\omega^2$ and $me\alpha$.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius $R$ rolls without slipping along a horizontal road. Which relation links the acceleration of its centre $a_G$ to its angular acceleration $\alpha$?

distractorRationale.b: The constraint is linear in $\alpha$; $\alpha^2$ is not involved.
distractorRationale.c: This inverts the relation and has the wrong dimensions.
distractorRationale.d: This is the acceleration of the top point of the wheel relative to the ground in some textbook configurations, not of the centre.

questions.explanation: The contact point has zero velocity, so the centre moves at $v_G=R\omega$ and differentiating gives $a_G=R\alpha$. This extra equation is what lets friction be found from the three planar equations.

questions.stem: A thin hoop (mass 4 kg, radius 0.30 m, $I_G=mR^2$) rolls without slipping on a horizontal surface under a horizontal force of 24 N applied at its centre. Find the acceleration of the centre in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Translation gives $P-F=ma$ and rotation gives $FR=mR^2(a/R)$, so $F=ma$. Hence $P=2ma$ and $a=24/(2\cdot4)=3.0$ m/s$^2$, with friction $F=12$ N.

questions.stem: A drive wheel (solid cylinder, mass 10 kg, radius 0.20 m) rolls without slip on level ground and carries no other load. A motor applies a driving torque of 15 N m to the wheel. Taking friction at the ground as the only horizontal force on the wheel, find the acceleration of its centre in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Friction $F$ acts forward: $F=ma$. Moments about the centre give $M-FR=\tfrac12mR^2(a/R)$, so $M=FR+\tfrac12mRa=\tfrac32mRa$. Then $a=15/(1.5\cdot10\cdot0.2)=5.0$ m/s$^2$, which needs $F=50$ N or $\mu_s\ge0.51$.

questions.stem: A load is lowered on a cable from a winch drum and is accelerating downward. How does the cable tension $T$ compare with the weight $mg$?

distractorRationale.a: That holds only for constant velocity or at rest.
distractorRationale.c: That would decelerate the load, i.e. accelerate it upward.
distractorRationale.d: This would be free fall; the drum inertia prevents it.

questions.explanation: For downward acceleration $a$, $mg-T=ma$, so $T=m(g-a)<mg$. The drum's rotational inertia keeps the tension positive.

questions.stem: A winch drum of radius 0.30 m and inertia 3.6 kg m$^2$ lowers an 80 kg load on a light inextensible cable. Ignoring bearing friction and taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the cable tension in N while the load accelerates freely downward.
questions.explanation: The drum's equivalent mass is $I/r^2=3.6/0.09=40$ kg, so $a=80(9.81)/120=6.54$ m/s$^2$. Then $T=40(6.54)=261.6$ N, which equals $m(g-a)=80(3.27)$.

questions.stem: For a winch lowering a load of fixed mass, the drum inertia $I$ is doubled with the same drum radius. What happens to the acceleration $a$ and cable tension $T$ of the load?

distractorRationale.a: A larger drum inertia resists spin-up, so the load cannot accelerate faster.
distractorRationale.b: Smaller $a$ means more of the weight is carried by the cable, so $T$ rises.

questions.explanation: With $a=mg/(m+I/r^2)$ a larger $I$ reduces $a$. Since $T=m(g-a)$, a smaller $a$ gives a larger $T$, approaching $mg$ for a very heavy drum.

questions.stem: A rotor of mass 12 kg has its centre of mass 2.5 mm from the axis of a vertical shaft (so its weight acts along the shaft axis). It turns at constant 3000 rev/min. Find the magnitude of the bearing force in N needed to hold the rotor, from the unbalance alone.
questions.explanation: The angular speed is $\omega=3000\cdot2\pi/60=314.2$ rad/s. With $\alpha=0$ the force is $me\omega^2=12(0.0025)(314.2)^2=2961$ N, directed toward the shaft axis from the centre of mass.

questions.stem: A rotor with an off-centre centre of mass (distance $e$ from the pin) spins at constant angular speed $\omega$ in the horizontal plane, with gravity along the shaft axis. Which statement about the pin reaction is correct?

options.text: It has magnitude $me\omega^2$ and points away from the pin
It has magnitude $me\alpha$ and is tangential
It has magnitude $me\omega^2$, points from G toward the pin, and no driving moment is needed

questions.correctOptionText: It has magnitude $me\omega^2$, points from G toward the pin, and no driving moment is needed

distractorRationale.b: The net force on the body must point toward the centre of its circular path.
distractorRationale.c: That is the tangential part, which vanishes at constant speed.

questions.explanation: Centre of mass G moves in a circle of radius $e$ with acceleration $e\omega^2$ toward the pin. Newton's second law then demands a pin force $me\omega^2$ toward the pin, and with $\alpha=0$ the moment equation requires no driving moment.

questions.stem: Explain why, for a wheel rolling without slip, the friction force at the contact point is not given by $\mu_kN$ and does no work, and describe how the rolling constraint is used to solve for the wheel's acceleration.
markingGuide: Contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the ground, so friction is static
States $F\le\mu_sN$ and that $F$ takes the value required by equilibrium of the equations
Notes the point of application has zero velocity, so the friction force does no work
Uses translational and rotational equations plus the constraint to solve for $a$, $\alpha$ and $F$, then checks $F\le\mu_sN$
questions.explanation: The three planar equations have four unknowns ($a_G$, $\alpha$, $F$ and possibly $N$ is known from the vertical equation). The constraint closes the set, and the final check on $F/N$ confirms that no-slip was a valid assumption.

questions.stem: A pump impeller has an off-centre centre of mass and the bearings are failing. Explain how the bearing loads depend on speed, why the loads change direction as the shaft turns, and give two ways to reduce them.
markingGuide: Force from unbalance is $F=me\omega^2$, proportional to the square of speed
The force vector rotates with the shaft, so bearing load is cyclic, causing fatigue and vibration
Contrasts with the constant weight load that does not rotate
Reduce $e$ by balancing: add or remove mass until G lies on the axis
Or reduce $\omega$ or mass; adding counter-mass in a balancing plane is acceptable
questions.explanation: Because the load is proportional to $\omega^2$, doubling the speed multiplies the unbalance force by four. Balancing makes $e\approx0$, removing the rotating force at its source.
